title: Let me see You
hook: Musa asks to see Allah, the mountain crumbles, and he falls fainting, then repents (7:143)
carry: the mountain could not bear it

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shu'ayb and the scales. Your line was full measure. Today, surah seven reaches Musa, and a request nobody expects.

Musa has been called from beside a fire, has stood before Pharaoh, has watched the sea split. Now Allah sets him an appointment: thirty nights on the mountain, completed with ten more, forty in all. He goes up alone, and there Allah speaks to him. That's why Muslims give Musa the title kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to. It might seem like enough. Musa, standing in that conversation, asks for one thing more.
screen: `FORTY NIGHTS ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `KALIMULLAH — THE ONE ALLAH SPOKE TO.` → `ONE THING MORE.`

segments.voice: Verse one-forty-three. Musa says: rabbi arini anzur ilayk. My Lord, show me, so that I may look at You. A request made out of longing, not arrogance. The answer comes, in Pickthall's words: “Thou wilt not see Me, but gaze upon the mountain!” If it stays firm in its place, then you will see Me. Then Allah reveals His glory to the mountain, and the mountain is crushed, made level, turned to dust. Musa falls down unconscious. When he comes to, his first words are: glory be to You. I turn to You in repentance, and I am the first of the believers. What does he repent of? Some commentators say it wasn't a sin, exactly, but asking for more than a human being can bear. The text doesn't scold the longing. It shows its size with a mountain that couldn't hold it. Jews and Christians know a related scene in Exodus, where Moses asks to see God's glory and is told no one can see God's face and live; each tradition tells it in its own way. And the swoon echoes later. A hadith in Bukhari says that on the Day of Resurrection, when people fall unconscious, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ will be the first to wake, and he'll find Musa already there, holding the side of the Throne. The Prophet said he didn't know whether Musa woke first, or was spared that swoon because of the one on the mountain. Musa's longing, it seems, wasn't wasted.
screen: `MY LORD, SHOW ME.` · `LOOK AT THE MOUNTAIN.` · `CRUSHED TO DUST; MUSA FALLS.` · `GLORY TO YOU; I TURN TO YOU.` · then, large: `THE MOUNTAIN COULD NOT BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: Look up at something vast, a big sky, a tall tree, a high ceiling, or picture one, and notice your size next to it. Then remember the mountain in the story, far larger than you, unable to bear a glimpse of the glory, and let the smallness feel safe, not crushing.
Arini, show me. Musa's request on the mountain, answered with a crumbling peak, a swoon, and glory to You. Today's word.
Your line: the mountain could not bear it. Musa asked anyway, out of longing. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Musa as kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to; the scene at the mountain is often recited and taught as a picture of longing for God, and of His majesty beyond what creation can bear.

what a scholar hears: lan tarani, you will not see Me, is central to the ru'yah debate; Ash'aris read lan as this-world only, Mu'tazilis as never.

chat.says: Was Musa wrong to ask to see God on the mountain?
options: The text doesn't scold the longing; it shows its size: the mountain couldn't bear the glory.
Yes, he was punished for it, and lost his place as a prophet after that day.
No, he saw Allah clearly on the mountain, and then told the people about it.
